sk: ॐ ब्रह्मविदाप्नोति परम् तदेषाऽभ्युक्ता सत्यं ज्ञानमनन्तं ब्रह्म यो वेद निहितं गुहायां परमे व्योमन् सोऽश्नुते सर्वान् कामान् सह ब्रह्मणा विपश्चितेति तस्माद्वा एतस्मादात्मन आकाशः संभूतः आकाशाद्वायुः वायोरग्निः अग्नेरापः अद्भ्यः पृथिवी पृथिव्या ओषधयः ओषधीभ्योऽन्नम् अन्नात्पुरुषः ||
ro: oṁ · brahma-vit · āpnoti · param · tat · eṣā · abhyuktā · satyaṁ · jñānam · anantaṁ · brahma · yaḥ · veda · nihitaṁ · guhāyāṁ · parame · vyoman · saḥ · aśnute · sarvān · kāmān · saha · brahmaṇā · vipaścitā · iti · tasmāt · vā · etasmāt · ātmanaḥ · ākāśaḥ · saṁbhūtaḥ · ākāśāt · vāyuḥ · vāyoḥ · agniḥ · agneḥ · āpaḥ · adbhyaḥ · pṛthivī · pṛthivyāḥ · oṣadhayaḥ · oṣadhībhyaḥ · annam · annāt · puruṣaḥ ||
hi: ॐ — ब्रह्मवित् (the knower of Brahman / ब्रह्म को जानने वाला) आप्नोति (attains / प्राप्त करता है) परम् (the highest / परम)। यही (तत्) इस (एषा) उक्ति (abhyuktā / verse / श्लोक) में कहा गया है: 'सत्यं ज्ञानम् अनन्तं ब्रह्म' — ब्रह्म सत्य (truth / सत्य) है, ज्ञान (knowledge / ज्ञान) है, अनन्त (infinite / अनन्त) है। जो (यः) इसे (ब्रह्म को) गुहा (cave of the heart / हृदय-गुहा) में, परम व्योमन् (the highest space / परम आकाश) में, निहित (hidden / छिपा हुआ) जानता है (वेद) — वह (सः) सर्वान् कामान् (all desires / सभी कामनाओं को) अश्नुते (attains / प्राप्त करता है) — विपश्चित् (the all-knowing / सर्वज्ञ) ब्रह्म के साथ (सह ब्रह्मणा)। उस (तस्मात्) इस (एतस्मात्) आत्मन् (Self / आत्मा) से आकाश (space) संभूत (arose / उत्पन्न हुआ)। आकाश से वायु (wind)। वायु से अग्नि (fire)। अग्नि से आपः (waters)। जल से पृथिवी (earth)। पृथिवी से ओषधि (herbs / plants)। ओषधियों से अन्न (food)। अन्न से पुरुष (the person / पुरुष)।
en: Om. The knower of Brahman (brahma-vit) attains the highest (param). Regarding this, the following verse is declared: 'Brahman is truth (satya), knowledge (jñāna), infinite (ananta).' He who knows It as hidden (nihita) in the cave [of the heart] (guhā), in the highest space (parame vyoman) — he attains all desires (sarvān kāmān) together with the all-knowing Brahman (saha brahmaṇā vipaścitā). From that Self (ātman), space (ākāśa) arose. From space, wind (vāyu). From wind, fire (agni). From fire, waters (āpaḥ). From waters, earth (pṛthivī). From earth, herbs (oṣadhi). From herbs, food (anna). From food, the person (puruṣa).

ws.h: ब्रह्म को जानने वाला / the knower of Brahman
ws.e: the knower of Brahman — brahma + √vid (to know); the one who has direct knowledge (not mere intellectual understanding) of Brahman; this knowledge is transformative — the knower ATTAINS Brahman, not just learns about it

ws.h: सत्य ज्ञान अनन्त / truth knowledge infinite
ws.e: truth, knowledge, infinite — the triple definition of Brahman; not three separate qualities but three aspects of one reality: satya (reality/truth — as opposed to the illusory), jñāna (pure consciousness/knowledge — as opposed to inert matter), ananta (infinite/unlimited — as opposed to the finite); the most important definition of Brahman in the Upanishads

ws.h: हृदय-गुहा में / in the cave [of the heart]
ws.e: in the cave — guhā = cave/secret place; refers to the 'cave of the heart' (hṛdaya-guhā) — the innermost recess of one's being where Brahman/ātman is hidden; cf. Kaṭha 1.2.12: 'the Self, hidden in the cave of the heart'

ws.h: सर्वज्ञ / all-knowing / supremely wise
ws.e: all-knowing / supremely wise — vi + paś + cit; an epithet of Brahman as omniscient; the knower attains desires 'together with' (saha) the all-knowing Brahman — i.e., by becoming one with Brahman

ws.h: ओषधि / वनस्पति / herbs / plants
ws.e: herbs / plants — specifically plants that bear fruit once and then die (annuals); the Taittirīya places plants in the creation sequence between earth and food — earth produces plants, plants produce food, food produces the person

ws.h: पुरुष / व्यक्ति / the person / the being
ws.e: the person / the individual being — the human being as the culmination of the creation sequence; puru + √ṣā (to fill); the being made of food (anna-maya) — the starting point for the five-sheath analysis that follows

gr: The opening declaration and the creation sequence: this mantra opens the Brahmānandavallī (the 'Section on the Bliss of Brahman') with two foundational teachings. Part 1 — The definition of Brahman: 'satyaṁ jñānam anantaṁ brahma' — Brahman is truth, knowledge, infinite. This is the most important lakṣaṇa (definition) of Brahman in the Upanishads. Three words, each negating a possible misunderstanding: (a) satya (truth/reality) — Brahman is not unreal or illusory; it is the REAL. (b) jñāna (knowledge/consciousness) — Brahman is not inert matter; it is pure consciousness. (c) ananta (infinite/unlimited) — Brahman is not limited by space, time, or form; it is without boundary. Part 2 — The creation sequence: from the Self (ātman), the elements emerge in a cascade: ātman → ākāśa (space) → vāyu (wind) → agni (fire) → āpaḥ (waters) → pṛthivī (earth) → oṣadhi (plants) → anna (food) → puruṣa (person). This is the sṛṣṭi-krama (order of creation) — a systematic emanation from the subtlest (ākāśa/space) to the grossest (anna/food → puruṣa/person). It sets up the five-sheath doctrine that follows: the puruṣa (person) made of food will be analysed layer by layer, from the outermost (annamaya) to the innermost (ānandamaya).
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_2.1.1 — The definition 'satyaṁ jñānam anantaṁ brahma' is the Taittirīya's mahāvākya-like statement — though not traditionally counted among the four mahāvākyas, it is arguably the most philosophically precise definition of Brahman in the Upanishads. Shankara's commentary on this passage is one of his most detailed and philosophically important — he analyses how the three words function as a svarūpa-lakṣaṇa (essential definition) by mutual delimitation (anyonya-viśeṣaṇa): each word excludes possible misidentifications. The creation sequence (ātman → ākāśa → vāyu → agni → āpaḥ → pṛthivī → oṣadhi → anna → puruṣa) parallels similar sequences in the Chāndogya (6.2.3-4) and the Aitareya (1.1.1-4), though each Upanishad orders the elements slightly differently. The phrase 'nihitaṁ guhāyām' (hidden in the cave) echoes the Kaṭha (1.2.12, 1.3.1) and the Muṇḍaka (2.1.10) — Brahman is simultaneously the cosmic Absolute AND the innermost Self hidden in the heart.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'सत्यं ज्ञानम् अनन्तम्' = ब्रह्म का स्वरूप-लक्षण (essential definition) — तीन शब्द परस्पर विशेषण (mutual qualification) द्वारा ब्रह्म को परिभाषित करते हैं: सत्य (real, not illusory) + ज्ञान (consciousness, not inert) + अनन्त (infinite, not limited)। ब्रह्म = निर्गुण (without attributes) — ये तीन शब्द गुण नहीं बताते, बल्कि अन्य सबको नकारते (negate) हैं।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'satyaṁ jñānam anantam' = the essential definition (svarūpa-lakṣaṇa) of Brahman — three words define Brahman by mutual qualification: satya (real, not illusory) + jñāna (consciousness, not inert) + ananta (infinite, not limited). Brahman = nirguṇa (without attributes) — these three words do not ascribe qualities but negate all limitations.
advaita.ins: Three words — truth, knowledge, infinite — and each one rules out a mistake. Not unreal: satya. Not unconscious: jñāna. Not limited: ananta. Together they point to what Brahman IS by showing what it is NOT. And this Brahman is hidden in the cave of the heart — closer than close, yet overlooked.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'सत्यं ज्ञानम् अनन्तम्' = भगवान् के तीन स्वाभाविक गुण (three natural attributes of God): सत्य (eternal reality / नित्य सत्ता), ज्ञान (omniscience / सर्वज्ञता), अनन्त (infinite perfection / अनन्त पूर्णता)। ये गुण = भगवान् का स्वभाव (God's nature) — निर्गुण नहीं, सगुण (with attributes)। सृष्टि-क्रम = भगवान् की सृष्टि-लीला (God's creative play)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'satyaṁ jñānam anantam' = three natural attributes of God: satya (eternal reality), jñāna (omniscience), ananta (infinite perfection). These are God's nature — not attributeless (nirguṇa) but full of auspicious attributes (saguṇa). The creation sequence = God's creative play.
vishisht.ins: God is truth — eternally real. God is knowledge — omniscient. God is infinite — without limit. These aren't negations but descriptions of His glory. And from this glorious God, the entire creation cascades — space, wind, fire, water, earth, plants, food, the person. Every layer is His.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'सत्यं ज्ञानम् अनन्तम्' = चेतना (consciousness) के तीन मूल आयाम: सत्य = सत्-चेतना (existence-consciousness), ज्ञान = चित्-शक्ति (consciousness-force), अनन्त = आनन्द-विस्तार (bliss-extension / infinite self-delight)। सृष्टि-क्रम = चेतना का अवरोहण (descent of consciousness) — सूक्ष्म से स्थूल (subtle to gross)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'satyaṁ jñānam anantam' = three fundamental dimensions of consciousness: satya = existence-consciousness, jñāna = consciousness-force, ananta = bliss-extension / infinite self-delight. The creation sequence = the descent of consciousness from subtle to gross.
aurobindo.ins: Brahman as truth-knowledge-infinite maps to Sat-Chit-Ananda — existence, consciousness, bliss. From this triune consciousness, creation descends: space (the most subtle), then wind, fire, water, earth, plants, food, the person. Each step is consciousness condensing, becoming more material — but never ceasing to BE consciousness.

dp.q: 🔍 'Satyaṁ jñānam anantaṁ brahma' — the triple definition
dp.a: The phrase 'satyaṁ jñānam anantaṁ brahma' is arguably the most philosophically precise definition of Brahman in the entire Upanishadic corpus: Why three words? Each word eliminates a possible misidentification of Brahman: (1) Satya (truth/reality): eliminates the possibility that Brahman is unreal (mithyā) or illusory — Brahman is the one thing that is absolutely REAL. Everything else may be subject to change or dissolution, but Brahman is that which never ceases to be. (2) Jñāna (knowledge/consciousness): eliminates the possibility that Brahman is inert matter (jaḍa) — Brahman is pure consciousness, not a thing but the awareness in which all things appear. This is not 'knowledge of something' (viṣaya-jñāna) but knowledge as such (svarūpa-jñāna) — awareness itself. (3) Ananta (infinite/unlimited): eliminates the possibility that Brahman is finite or bounded — not limited by space (it is everywhere), not limited by time (it is eternal), not limited by objects (it is not one thing among others). Shankara's analysis: Shankara reads these as anyonya-viśeṣaṇa (mutual qualifiers) — not three separate qualities but three ways of pointing to ONE reality. 'The satya that is jñāna and ananta = Brahman.' Each word refines the meaning of the others. Connection to Sat-Chit-Ānanda: later Vedāntic tradition maps this triple definition onto the more familiar Sat-Chit-Ānanda: satya ≈ sat (existence), jñāna ≈ cit (consciousness), ananta ≈ ānanda (bliss/infinity). The Taittirīya itself will develop the ānanda (bliss) aspect in mantras 7-8 of the Brahmānandavallī.

dp.q: 🔍 The creation sequence — from Self to food to person
dp.a: The creation sequence ātman → ākāśa → vāyu → agni → āpaḥ → pṛthivī → oṣadhi → anna → puruṣa is one of the Upanishads' most systematic accounts of cosmogony: The principle: creation proceeds from the subtlest to the grossest — from pure being (ātman) through increasingly dense states of matter to the physical person made of food. Each element emerges FROM the one before it — not as a separate creation but as a condensation or densification. The sequence: (1) Ātman/Brahman: the source — pure consciousness, uncreated. (2) Ākāśa (space): the first emergence — the most subtle element, space itself, the container of all. (3) Vāyu (wind/air): movement within space — the principle of motion and energy. (4) Agni (fire): heat/light — the transformative principle. (5) Āpaḥ (waters): the fluid element — the basis of life. (6) Pṛthivī (earth): the solid element — stable matter. (7) Oṣadhi (plants/herbs): the first life-forms — converting earth and water into living matter. (8) Anna (food): the sustenance of animal life — plants become food. (9) Puruṣa (person): the human being — made of food, sustained by food. The setup: this sequence establishes the 'annamaya puruṣa' (the person made of food) — which becomes the OUTERMOST layer in the five-sheath analysis. The Brahmānandavallī will now systematically peel back the layers: food-sheath → breath-sheath → mind-sheath → knowledge-sheath → bliss-sheath → Brahman at the core.

sk: स वा एष पुरुषोऽन्नरसमयः तस्येदमेव शिरः अयं दक्षिणः पक्षः अयमुत्तरः पक्षः अयमात्मा अयमुच्छ्यः प्रतिष्ठा तदप्येष श्लोको भवति ||
ro: saḥ · vā · eṣaḥ · puruṣaḥ · anna-rasa-mayaḥ · tasya · idam · eva · śiraḥ · ayaṁ · dakṣiṇaḥ · pakṣaḥ · ayam · uttaraḥ · pakṣaḥ · ayam · ātmā · ayam · ucchyaḥ · pratiṣṭhā · tat · api · eṣaḥ · ślokaḥ · bhavati ||
hi: वह (सः) यह (एषः) पुरुष (person) अन्नरसमय (made of the essence of food / अन्न-रस से बना हुआ) है। इसका (तस्य) यह (इदम्) ही शिरः (head / शीर्ष) है। यह (अयम्) दक्षिण पक्ष (right wing/side / दाहिना पक्ष)। यह उत्तर पक्ष (left wing/side / बायाँ पक्ष)। यह (अयम्) आत्मा (the body/trunk / मध्य भाग / the self)। यह (अयम्) उच्छ्यः प्रतिष्ठा (the tail, the support / पुच्छ — आधार)। इस विषय में (तत् अपि) यह (एषः) श्लोक (verse) है —
en: This person (puruṣa) is indeed made of the essence of food (anna-rasa-maya). Of this [person-shaped form], this is the head (śiras). This is the right wing (dakṣiṇa pakṣa). This is the left wing (uttara pakṣa). This is the trunk/self (ātmā). This is the tail, the support (ucchya pratiṣṭhā). Regarding this, there is this verse —

ws.h: अन्न-रस से बना / made of the essence of food
ws.e: made of the essence of food — anna (food) + rasa (essence/juice) + maya (made of/consisting of); the physical body is understood as a condensation of the nutritive essence of food; this is the first and outermost of the five kośas (sheaths)

ws.h: पक्ष / पंख / wing / side
ws.e: wing / side — the kośa (sheath) is visualised in the shape of a bird: head, two wings, body/trunk, and tail; this bird-shape applies to ALL five sheaths, each nested inside the previous one like a bird inside a bird

ws.h: पुच्छ — आधार / tail — the support/foundation
ws.e: tail — the support/foundation — ucchya (tail, from ud + √ci) + pratiṣṭhā (support/foundation/base); the tail of the bird-shaped kośa is its foundation — what it rests upon; each sheath's pratiṣṭhā is identified with a specific principle

ws.h: मध्य भाग / शरीर / trunk / self / body
ws.e: trunk / body / self — here ātmā is used in its physical sense: the central body or trunk of the bird-shaped form; in the kośa framework, the ātmā of each sheath is its core identity — what the sheath fundamentally IS

gr: The first sheath — annamaya (made of food): this mantra introduces the annarasamaya puruṣa — the person made of the essence of food — and establishes the BIRD-SHAPE template that all five sheaths will follow. The bird-shape (vihaga-ākāra): each kośa is described as having five parts shaped like a bird: (1) śiras (head), (2) dakṣiṇa pakṣa (right wing), (3) uttara pakṣa (left wing), (4) ātmā (trunk/body), (5) ucchya/pratiṣṭhā (tail/support). This template will be repeated for ALL five sheaths — prāṇamaya, manomaya, vijñānamaya, ānandamaya — with different principles mapped to each part. Why a bird? The bird shape is significant: (a) A bird has an obvious head, two symmetrical wings, a body, and a tail — a clear five-part structure. (b) The wings suggest EXTENSION — the sheath extends outward from a central core. (c) The tail as pratiṣṭhā (support/foundation) — each sheath rests on something, just as a bird balances on its tail. The annamaya kośa: the outermost sheath is made of anna-rasa (the essence of food). The physical body IS food transformed — built from what we eat. This is the starting point: the grossest, most visible layer of the person.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_2.2.1 — The five-sheath (pañca-kośa) doctrine is the Taittirīya's most influential and original contribution to Indian philosophy. The bird-shape template for each kośa is unique to the Taittirīya — no other Upanishad uses this structure. The specific parts (head, right wing, left wing, trunk, tail/support) for the annamaya kośa are not explicitly named in this introductory verse — they are stated in the accompanying verse (which declares anna as the head, etc.). The word 'annarasamaya' uses 'rasa' (essence/juice) rather than just 'anna' — emphasising that the body is not made of crude food but of food's nutritive ESSENCE, transformed through digestion. The pratiṣṭhā (support/foundation) concept is important: each sheath 'rests' on a more fundamental principle. The annamaya rests on food-production (earth/agriculture); the deeper sheaths will rest on progressively more subtle principles.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — अन्नरसमय = स्थूल शरीर (gross body) = अन्न (food) के रस (essence) से निर्मित। यह पहला कोश (first sheath) = सबसे बाहरी आवरण (outermost covering)। आत्मा (Self) इसके भीतर है — जैसे तलवार म्यान (sheath) में। पक्षी-आकृति (bird-shape) = कोश की संरचना — शिर, दो पक्ष, मध्य, पुच्छ।
advaita.en: Shankara says annarasamaya = the gross body (sthūla śarīra) = formed from the essence of food. This is the first kośa (sheath) = the outermost covering. The Self (ātman) is within it — like a sword in its scabbard. The bird-shape = the structure of the kośa — head, two wings, body, tail.
advaita.ins: The physical body is the first sheath — the outermost layer. It's made of food, shaped like a bird. But inside this food-body is another self — made of breath. And inside that, another. The Taittirīya is about to peel back five layers to reach the core.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — अन्नरसमय पुरुष = भगवान् का अन्न-शरीर (God's food-body) — शरीर = भगवान् का बाह्य रूप (outer form of God)। पाँच कोश = भगवान् के शरीर की पाँच परतें (five layers of God's body) — बाहर से भीतर — सबमें भगवान्।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says annarasamaya puruṣa = God's food-body — the body = the outer form of God. Five sheaths = five layers of God's body — outer to inner — God is present in all.
vishisht.ins: The physical body — made of food — is the outermost form of God. The Taittirīya will show you five nested layers, each more interior, each closer to God. The food-body is where you start — but God is already here, as the innermost Self within it.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — अन्नरसमय = भौतिक चेतना (physical consciousness) — चेतना का सबसे स्थूल रूप (grossest form of consciousness)। पाँच कोश = चेतना के पाँच स्तर (five planes of consciousness) — भौतिक से आनन्दमय तक। शरीर = चेतना का भौतिक आवरण (physical sheath of consciousness)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says annarasamaya = physical consciousness — the grossest form of consciousness. Five sheaths = five planes of consciousness — from physical to bliss. The body = the physical sheath of consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: The body isn't just matter — it's consciousness in its most material form. The five sheaths aren't layers of covering but planes of consciousness, from the densest (food/physical) to the most luminous (bliss). Start with the body, but know that consciousness runs through every layer.

dp.q: 🔍 The pañca-kośa doctrine — five sheaths of the Self
dp.a: The pañca-kośa (five sheaths) doctrine is the Taittirīya Upanishad's most famous and influential teaching — a systematic analysis of the human person as five nested layers, each more subtle than the last: The five sheaths: (1) Annamaya kośa (food-sheath): the physical body — made of food (anna), sustained by food, returning to food (earth) at death. This is the outermost layer, visible and tangible. (2) Prāṇamaya kośa (breath-sheath): the vital body — the life-force (prāṇa) that animates the food-body. Without breath, the food-body is a corpse. (3) Manomaya kośa (mind-sheath): the mental body — thoughts, emotions, desires, the sense-mind that processes experience. (4) Vijñānamaya kośa (knowledge-sheath): the intellectual/intuitive body — the faculty of discernment (vijñāna), understanding, and will. (5) Ānandamaya kośa (bliss-sheath): the causal body — the deepest layer before the Self, characterised by bliss (ānanda). The nesting: each sheath is INSIDE the previous one — the breath-body pervades the food-body, the mind-body pervades the breath-body, and so on. The Self (ātman) is at the very centre — hidden within all five sheaths, like a kernel within five husks. The method: the Taittirīya's method is SUBTRACTIVE — it doesn't tell you what the Self IS but progressively strips away what it is NOT. 'You are not the food-body' — because the breath-body is more essential. 'You are not the breath-body' — because the mind is more essential. And so on, until only the Self remains. Legacy: the pañca-kośa model has influenced virtually every subsequent school of Indian philosophy — Advaita Vedānta, Yoga, Tantra, Āyurveda, and modern neo-Vedānta all use this framework.

dp.q: 🔍 The bird-shape — why the Taittirīya uses a bird template
dp.a: Each of the five sheaths is described in the shape of a bird (vihaga) with five parts — head, right wing, left wing, trunk, and tail (support): The five parts: (1) Śiras (head): the leading or governing principle — what directs the sheath. (2) Dakṣiṇa pakṣa (right wing): one of two complementary extensions. (3) Uttara pakṣa (left wing): the other complementary extension — together the wings represent the two sides that sustain and balance the sheath. (4) Ātmā (trunk/body): the central identity — the core of the sheath. (5) Puccha/pratiṣṭhā (tail/support): the foundation — what the sheath rests upon. Why a bird? (a) Symmetry: a bird has clear bilateral symmetry (two wings) with a governing head and a balancing tail — it's a natural template for any five-part structure. (b) The Vedic bird symbol: the bird (suparṇa/haṁsa) is a powerful Vedic symbol for the Self — the Ṛg Veda (1.164.20) and the Muṇḍaka (3.1.1) use the 'two birds on one tree' metaphor for the individual self and the cosmic Self. (c) Flight: a bird can fly — suggesting that the sheaths are not static shells but dynamic, living layers capable of movement and transformation. (d) Nesting: birds nest inside larger structures — and the kośas nest inside each other, each smaller (more subtle) bird inside a larger (grosser) one.

sk: अन्नाद्वै प्रजाः प्रजायन्ते याः काश्च पृथिवीꣳ श्रिताः अथो अन्नेनैव जीवन्ति अथैनदपि यन्त्यन्ततः अन्नं हि भूतानां ज्येष्ठम् तस्मात् सर्वौषधमुच्यते सर्वं वै तेऽन्नमाप्नुवन्ति येऽन्नं ब्रह्मोपासते अन्नं हि भूतानां ज्येष्ठम् तस्मात् सर्वौषधमुच्यते अन्नाद्भूतानि जायन्ते जातान्यन्नेन वर्धन्ते अद्यतेऽत्ति च भूतानि तस्मादन्नं तदुच्यत इति तस्माद्वा एतस्मादन्नरसमयात् अन्योऽन्तर आत्मा प्राणमयः तेनैष पूर्णः स वा एष पुरुषविध एव तस्य पुरुषविधताम् अन्वयं पुरुषविधः प्राणो ह्यस्य शिरः व्यानो दक्षिणः पक्षः अपान उत्तरः पक्षः आकाश आत्मा पृथिवी पुच्छं प्रतिष्ठा तदप्येष श्लोको भवति ||

hi: अन्न (food) से ही (वै) सभी प्रजाएँ (beings / सभी जीव) प्रजायन्ते (are born / जन्म लेती हैं) — जो कोई भी (याः काश्च) पृथिवी (earth) पर आश्रित (श्रिताः) हैं। फिर (अथो) अन्न से ही जीवन्ति (they live / जीवित रहती हैं)। फिर (अथ) अन्त में (अन्ततः) उसी (एनत्) में ही (अपि) यन्ति (they enter / प्रवेश करती हैं / लौट जाती हैं)। अन्न (food) ही (हि) भूतों (beings / प्राणियों) में ज्येष्ठ (eldest / सबसे पहला / सर्वप्रथम) है। इसलिए (तस्मात्) सर्वौषधम् (the medicine of all / सबकी औषधि) उच्यते (is called / कहा जाता है)। जो अन्न को ब्रह्म (Brahman) के रूप में उपासते (meditate) करते हैं — वे (ते) सर्व (all) अन्न प्राप्त करते हैं (आप्नुवन्ति)। [पुनः] अन्न ही भूतों में ज्येष्ठ है, इसलिए सर्वौषध कहा जाता है। अन्न से भूत (beings) जायन्ते (are born / जन्मते हैं)। जन्मे हुए (जातानि) अन्न से वर्धन्ते (grow / बढ़ते हैं)। [अन्न] अद्यते (is eaten / खाया जाता है) और (च) भूतों को अत्ति (eats / खाता है) — इसलिए (तस्मात्) अन्नम् (food) तत् (that) उच्यते (is called / कहा जाता है)। उस (तस्मात्) इस (एतस्मात्) अन्नरसमय (made of food-essence) से अन्यः (another / अन्य) अन्तर (inner / भीतरी) आत्मा (self) है — प्राणमय (made of breath / प्राण से बना)। उससे (तेन) यह (एषः) पूर्ण (filled / भरा हुआ) है। वह (सः) यह (एषः) पुरुषविध (person-shaped / पुरुष के आकार का) ही (एव) है। उसकी (तस्य) पुरुषविधता (person-shape) के अनुसार (अन्वयम्) [यह भी] पुरुषविध है। प्राण (prāṇa / out-breath) ही (हि) इसका (अस्य) शिर (head / शीर्ष)। व्यान (vyāna / diffused breath) = दक्षिण पक्ष (right wing)। अपान (apāna / in-breath) = उत्तर पक्ष (left wing)। आकाश (space) = आत्मा (trunk / body)। पृथिवी (earth) = पुच्छ प्रतिष्ठा (tail-support / आधार)। इस विषय में यह श्लोक है —
en: From food indeed all beings are born — whatever [beings] dwell on earth. Then by food they live. Then into food they enter at the end. Food indeed is the eldest (jyeṣṭha) of beings; therefore it is called the medicine of all (sarva-auṣadha). Those who meditate on food as Brahman — they obtain all food. Food is the eldest of beings; therefore it is called the medicine of all. From food beings are born; once born, by food they grow. It is eaten (adyate) and it eats (atti) beings — therefore it is called 'anna' (food). Other than this [self] made of food-essence, there is an inner self made of breath (prāṇamaya). By that, this [food-self] is filled (pūrṇa). That too is person-shaped (puruṣa-vidha). Conforming to its person-shape, this [inner self] is [also] person-shaped. Prāṇa (out-breath) is its head. Vyāna (diffused breath) is the right wing. Apāna (in-breath) is the left wing. Space (ākāśa) is the trunk (ātmā). Earth (pṛthivī) is the tail-support (puccha-pratiṣṭhā). Regarding this, there is this verse —

ws.h: सबसे पहला / eldest / first-born
ws.e: eldest / first-born / most senior — superlative of jyā (elder); food is called the 'eldest of beings' because in the creation sequence, food precedes the person — food exists before the beings it sustains; also = most fundamental/primary

ws.h: सबकी औषधि / medicine of all / remedy for all
ws.e: medicine/remedy for all — sarva (all) + auṣadha (medicine/herb); food is called 'the medicine of all' because it is the universal remedy — hunger, weakness, disease are all addressed by food; food sustains, heals, and restores

ws.h: खाया जाता है / खाता है / is eaten / eats
ws.e: is eaten AND eats — the famous Taittirīya etymology of 'anna': food (anna) is so called because it 'is eaten' (adyate — passive of √ad) AND 'eats' (atti — active of √ad) beings. Food eats beings in the sense that beings return to food/earth at death — the cycle is reciprocal

ws.h: प्राण से बना / made of breath / consisting of vital force
ws.e: made of breath / consisting of vital force — prāṇa (breath/life-force) + maya (made of/consisting of); the second kośa (sheath) — the vital body that animates the food-body; more subtle than the annamaya, it pervades and fills it

gr: The hymn to food and the second sheath (prāṇamaya): this long mantra has two parts. Part 1 — The hymn to anna (food): a remarkable celebration of food as a cosmic principle: (a) From food all beings are born, by food they live, into food they return at death — the complete cycle. (b) Food is the 'eldest' (jyeṣṭha) of beings — more fundamental than the creatures it sustains. (c) Food is 'sarva-auṣadha' (the medicine of all) — the universal remedy. (d) The etymology: anna is called 'anna' because it 'is eaten' (adyate) AND 'eats' (atti) beings — a reciprocal relationship. The eater and the eaten are caught in a cycle. Part 2 — The prāṇamaya kośa (breath-sheath): different from and INNER to the annamaya, there is a self made of prāṇa (breath/vital force). It fills the food-body ('tena eṣaḥ pūrṇaḥ' — by it, this is filled) and is also person-shaped (puruṣa-vidha). Its bird-parts: prāṇa (out-breath) = head, vyāna (diffused breath) = right wing, apāna (in-breath) = left wing, ākāśa (space) = trunk, pṛthivī (earth) = tail/support. The nesting: the prāṇamaya is INSIDE the annamaya, filling it — the breath-body pervades the food-body. Without breath, the food-body is inert. The breath-body gives the food-body life.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_2.2.1-2.3.1 — The hymn to food anticipates the Bhṛguvallī (3.1-10) where food (anna) will be Bhṛgu's first realisation of Brahman. The etymology 'adyate atti ca' (is eaten and eats) is a classic Upanishadic nirukta (etymology) — not a scientific derivation but a semantic meditation on the word's meaning. The reciprocal 'eating' is profound: food sustains life, but life returns to become food for other life and for the earth — the eater becomes the eaten. This anticipates the Bṛhadāraṇyaka's 'aham annam, aham annam, aham annam; aham annādaḥ' (I am food, I am food, I am food; I am the eater of food — 1.4.6). The prāṇamaya kośa's bird-parts map the three main prāṇas onto the bird-shape: prāṇa (head = governing breath), vyāna (right wing = pervading breath), apāna (left wing = downward breath), with space (ākāśa) as the trunk and earth (pṛthivī) as the support.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — अन्न-स्तुति (praise of food) = अन्नमय कोश (food-sheath) की महत्ता (importance) — परन्तु यह आत्मा (Self) नहीं। अन्नमय = जड़ (inert) — इसलिए इसके भीतर प्राणमय (breath-self) = अधिक सूक्ष्म (more subtle)। प्रत्येक कोश = बाहरी कोश से अधिक सूक्ष्म — आत्मा (Self) = सबसे भीतर।
advaita.en: Shankara says the praise of food = the importance of the food-sheath — but it is NOT the Self. Annamaya = inert — therefore within it is the prāṇamaya (breath-self) = more subtle. Each kośa is more subtle than the outer one — the Self = the innermost.
advaita.ins: Food is remarkable — all beings are born from it, live by it, return to it. But the food-body is inert without breath. So look deeper: inside the food-sheath is the breath-sheath. This is the Taittirīya's method — peel back each layer, and the next one is more essential.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — अन्न = भगवान् का अन्न-रूप (God as food) — 'अन्नं ब्रह्मोपासते' = अन्न में भगवान् की उपासना। प्राणमय = भगवान् का प्राण-रूप (God as breath) — अन्नमय के भीतर — भगवान् हर कोश में।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says food = God as food — 'meditate on food as Brahman' = worship God in food. Prāṇamaya = God as breath — within the food-body — God is present in every sheath.
vishisht.ins: All beings are born from food, live by food, return to food. Meditate on food as God and you'll never lack. But inside the food-body, God is present as breath — the life-force that makes the body live. God is in every layer, every sheath.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — अन्न-स्तुति = भौतिक चेतना (physical consciousness) की गरिमा — पदार्थ (matter) = चेतना का आधार (base of consciousness)। प्राणमय = प्राण-चेतना (vital consciousness) — भौतिक से अधिक गतिशील (more dynamic) — शरीर को जीवन देने वाली।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says the praise of food = the dignity of physical consciousness — matter = the base of consciousness. Prāṇamaya = vital consciousness — more dynamic than physical — giving life to the body.
aurobindo.ins: Food is consciousness in its most material form — born from it, living by it, returning to it. But inside the food-body is the breath-body — vital consciousness, more dynamic, more alive. Each layer inward is consciousness becoming more awake, more itself.

dp.a: The Taittirīya's etymology of anna — 'adyate atti ca bhūtāni' (it is eaten AND it eats beings) — reveals a profound understanding of the food-cycle: The double meaning: anna comes from √ad (to eat). The Taittirīya plays on both forms: (a) adyate (is eaten — passive): food is consumed by beings. We eat food. (b) atti (eats — active): food 'eats' beings. How? At death, beings return to the earth and become food for other life. The eater becomes the eaten. The cycle: this is not just poetic — it describes the actual biological cycle: (1) Earth produces plants → plants become food → food becomes the body → the body dies → the body becomes earth → earth produces plants. The cycle has no beginning and no end. (2) At a more dramatic level: Time/Death 'eats' all beings — and Time/Death can be understood as the cosmic form of 'anna.' The Bṛhadāraṇyaka (1.2.5) identifies the cosmic eater (Death/Prajāpati) with the principle of consumption. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka echo: 'aham annam, aham annam, aham annam; aham annādaḥ, aham annādaḥ, aham annādaḥ' (I am food, I am food, I am food; I am the eater of food — BU 1.4.6). The realised person identifies with BOTH sides of the eating — they are the food AND the eater. This collapses the duality of consumer and consumed. The teaching: don't look at food as merely something you consume. You and food are in a RECIPROCAL relationship — you eat it now, it will eat you later. Understanding this dissolves the illusion of being the sovereign consumer and reveals the interconnected web of life.

dp.q: 🔍 The prāṇamaya kośa — breath as the second self
dp.a: The prāṇamaya kośa (breath-sheath) is the second layer — the vital body that animates the physical: Why breath is 'more self' than food: the food-body without breath is a corpse. Breath makes the difference between a living body and a dead one. Therefore breath is a more essential 'self' than food — it is what makes the food-body alive. The bird-parts: (1) Prāṇa (out-breath) = head: the governing breath — prāṇa leads the other vital functions. (2) Vyāna (diffused breath) = right wing: the pervading breath — circulates energy throughout the body. (3) Apāna (in-breath/downward breath) = left wing: the breath that moves inward/downward — governs intake and elimination. (4) Ākāśa (space) = trunk: the internal space of the body where breath operates. (5) Pṛthivī (earth) = tail/support: the physical earth that supports the breath-body — breath needs a material base. The filling principle: 'tena eṣaḥ pūrṇaḥ' — the prāṇamaya FILLS the annamaya. The breath-body pervades every part of the food-body. When breath withdraws from a limb, that limb goes numb; when breath withdraws from the body entirely, death occurs. The method continues: but even the prāṇamaya is not the final Self — it too is a sheath, a covering. Inside it is the manomaya (mind-sheath), which is more essential still.

sk: प्राणं देवा अनु प्राणन्ति मनुष्याः पशवश्च ये प्राणो हि भूतानामायुः तस्मात् सर्वायुषमुच्यते सर्वमेव त आयुर्यन्ति ये प्राणं ब्रह्मोपासते प्राणो हि भूतानामायुः तस्मात् सर्वायुषमुच्यत इति तस्माद्वा एतस्मात्प्राणमयात् अन्योऽन्तर आत्मा मनोमयः तेनैष पूर्णः स वा एष पुरुषविध एव तस्य पुरुषविधताम् अन्वयं पुरुषविधः यजुरेव शिरः ऋग्दक्षिणः पक्षः सामोत्तरः पक्षः आदेश आत्मा अथर्वाङ्गिरसः पुच्छं प्रतिष्ठा तदप्येष श्लोको भवति ||

hi: प्राण (breath / प्राण) के अनुसार (अनु) देवता (gods) प्राणन्ति (breathe / श्वास लेते हैं) — [और] मनुष्य (humans) और (च) पशु (animals) भी जो (ये) [पृथिवी पर हैं]। प्राण ही (हि) भूतों (beings) का आयुः (life-span / जीवन-काल) है। इसलिए (तस्मात्) सर्वायुषम् (the life of all / सबका आयु) उच्यते (is called / कहा जाता है)। जो (ये) प्राण को ब्रह्म (Brahman) के रूप में उपासते (meditate) करते हैं — वे (ते) सम्पूर्ण (सर्वम् एव) आयुः (life-span) प्राप्त करते हैं (यन्ति)। [पुनः] प्राण ही भूतों का आयुः है, इसलिए सर्वायुष कहा जाता है। उस (तस्मात्) इस (एतस्मात्) प्राणमय से अन्य (another / अन्य) अन्तर (inner) आत्मा (self) = मनोमय (made of mind / मन से बना) है। उससे यह पूर्ण (filled) है। वह पुरुषविध (person-shaped) ही है। उसकी पुरुषविधता के अनुसार [यह भी] पुरुषविध है। यजुः (Yajur mantras) ही (एव) [इसका] शिर (head)। ऋक् (Ṛg verses) = दक्षिण पक्ष (right wing)। साम (Sāma chants) = उत्तर पक्ष (left wing)। आदेश (instruction / precept / आदेश) = आत्मा (trunk)। अथर्वाङ्गिरसः (Atharva-Veda hymns) = पुच्छ प्रतिष्ठा (tail-support)। इस विषय में यह श्लोक है —
en: After breath (prāṇa), the gods breathe (anu prāṇanti), and so do humans and animals. Breath indeed is the life-span (āyus) of beings; therefore it is called 'the life of all' (sarva-āyuṣa). Those who meditate on breath as Brahman attain the full life-span (sarvam āyuḥ). Breath indeed is the life-span of beings; therefore it is called the life of all. Other than this [self] made of breath, there is an inner self made of mind (manomaya). By that, this [breath-self] is filled. That too is person-shaped. Conforming to its person-shape, this [inner self] is also person-shaped. The Yajur [mantras] are its head. The Ṛg [verses] are the right wing. The Sāma [chants] are the left wing. Instruction (ādeśa) is the trunk (ātmā). The Atharva-Aṅgirasa [hymns] are the tail-support. Regarding this, there is this verse —

ws.h: अनुसरण करके श्वास लेते हैं / breathe after / breathe following
ws.e: breathe after / breathe following — anu (after/following) + prāṇanti (they breathe); all beings — gods, humans, animals — breathe FOLLOWING prāṇa; prāṇa is the leader, all life follows its rhythm

ws.h: सबका आयु / the life of all
ws.e: the life of all / the universal life-span — sarva (all) + āyus (life/life-span); prāṇa is called the 'life of all' because it IS the life-force that determines how long any being lives; when prāṇa departs, life ends

ws.h: मन से बना / made of mind
ws.e: made of mind — manas (mind) + maya (made of); the third kośa — the mental body; the mind-sheath includes thoughts, emotions, desires, and the sense-mind (manas) that processes all sensory input

ws.h: आदेश / उपदेश / instruction / precept / directive
ws.e: instruction / precept / directive — ā + √diś (to point/direct); the Brāhmaṇa prose instructions that accompany the Vedic mantras; in the manomaya bird, ādeśa is the trunk (ātmā) — instruction is the CORE of the mind

ws.h: अथर्ववेद के मन्त्र / Atharva-Veda hymns
ws.e: the Atharva-Aṅgirasa hymns — the hymns attributed to Atharvan and Aṅgiras (the two legendary sages); = the Atharva Veda; placed as the tail/support of the manomaya because the Atharva Veda deals with practical/domestic applications — the foundation of mental life in the everyday world

gr: The hymn to breath and the third sheath (manomaya): this mantra follows the same pattern as the previous one — first praising the governing principle of the current sheath, then introducing the next deeper sheath. Part 1 — Praise of prāṇa: (a) All beings — gods, humans, animals — 'breathe after' (anu prāṇanti) prāṇa. Prāṇa is the leader; all life follows. (b) Prāṇa = āyus (life-span) of all beings. It is called 'sarva-āyuṣa' (the life of all). (c) Those who meditate on prāṇa as Brahman attain the full life-span. Part 2 — The manomaya kośa (mind-sheath): inside the prāṇamaya is a more subtle self made of manas (mind). It fills the breath-body and is also person-shaped. Its bird-parts are remarkable — they are the FOUR VEDAS plus instruction: yajus (head), ṛk (right wing), sāma (left wing), ādeśa (trunk), atharva-aṅgiras (tail/support). The Vedic mapping: the mind-sheath is described in terms of the Vedas because MIND is the faculty that receives, processes, and understands the Vedas. The mind is 'made of' the Vedas in the sense that the properly educated mind is structured by Vedic knowledge. The Yajur Veda is the head because this Upanishad BELONGS to the Yajur Veda — it gives precedence to its own tradition.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_2.3.1-2.4.1 — The praise of prāṇa ('prāṇaṁ devā anu prāṇanti') parallels the Kaṭha (2.3.2) and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka's contest of the prāṇas (6.1.1-14) where prāṇa proves to be the most essential faculty. The manomaya kośa's identification with the four Vedas is striking — it maps sacred knowledge onto the structure of the mind: Yajus = head (this Upanishad's own Veda), Ṛk = right wing, Sāma = left wing, Ādeśa (Brāhmaṇa instruction) = trunk, Atharva-Aṅgiras = tail/support. The four Vedas were traditionally associated with the four main priests: Yajur = Adhvaryu, Ṛg = Hotṛ, Sāma = Udgātṛ, Atharva = Brahmā. The placement of the Yajur as head reflects the Taittirīya's own Yajurvedic identity. Ādeśa (instruction/precept) as the trunk suggests that the CORE of the mind is not raw data but processed instruction — understanding, not mere information.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — प्राण = आयुः (life-span) — परन्तु प्राण भी आत्मा (Self) नहीं — क्योंकि प्राण = जड़ शक्ति (inert force) — बुद्धि (intelligence) रहित। इसलिए प्राणमय के भीतर मनोमय = मन (mind) = चेतन (conscious) = प्राण से सूक्ष्मतर (subtler than breath)। मनोमय = वेद-निर्मित (made of Vedas) — क्योंकि शुद्ध मन = वेद-ज्ञान से संस्कृत (refined by Vedic knowledge)।
advaita.en: Shankara says prāṇa = life-span — but prāṇa is NOT the Self either — because prāṇa = an inert force — devoid of intelligence. Therefore within the prāṇamaya is the manomaya = mind = conscious = subtler than breath. Manomaya = made of Vedas — because the purified mind = refined by Vedic knowledge.
advaita.ins: Breath sustains life — all beings breathe after it. But breath alone has no intelligence — it's a force, not a knower. So look deeper: inside the breath-body is the mind-body, structured by the four Vedas. Mind knows; breath merely animates. Another layer peeled back.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — प्राण = भगवान् की जीवन-शक्ति (God's life-force) — 'देवा अनु प्राणन्ति' = देवता भी भगवान् के प्राण का अनुसरण करते हैं। मनोमय = भगवान् का ज्ञान-रूप (God as knowledge) — वेदों से निर्मित — क्योंकि वेद = भगवद्-वाणी (God's word) = मन का सर्वोत्तम विषय (mind's highest content)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says prāṇa = God's life-force — even the gods breathe following God's breath. Manomaya = God as knowledge — made of the Vedas — because the Vedas = God's word = the highest content of the mind.
vishisht.ins: Even the gods breathe after God's breath — prāṇa is His life-force in everything. But deeper still is the mind — structured by the four Vedas, God's own word. The mind filled with God's scripture is the third layer: closer to God, more luminous than breath.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — प्राण = प्राणिक चेतना (vital consciousness) — जीवन-शक्ति — सभी जीवों को गतिशील करने वाली। मनोमय = मानसिक चेतना (mental consciousness) — प्राण से सूक्ष्मतर — विचार, भावना, संकल्प। वेदों से निर्मित = मन = दिव्य ज्ञान (divine knowledge) का ग्राहक (receiver)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says prāṇa = vital consciousness — the life-force that animates all beings. Manomaya = mental consciousness — subtler than prāṇa — thought, emotion, will. Made of Vedas = mind = the receiver of divine knowledge.
aurobindo.ins: Vital consciousness gives everything its drive, its push to live. But inside it is mental consciousness — thought, understanding, will. The mind-sheath is structured by sacred knowledge because the mind's highest function is to receive and process divine truth. Each layer inward is consciousness becoming more luminous.

dp.q: 🔍 The manomaya kośa — mind structured by the four Vedas
dp.a: The manomaya kośa (mind-sheath) is described with the four Vedas as its bird-parts — a mapping that reveals what the Taittirīya considers the IDEAL structure of the mind: The mapping: (1) Yajus (head): the Yajur Veda — sacrificial formulas, the science of ritual action. The head governs — the Yajur Veda is placed first because the Taittirīya belongs to this Veda, and because yajus represents PURPOSEFUL ACTION — the mind's governing function. (2) Ṛk (right wing): the Ṛg Veda — hymns of praise and invocation. One wing of the mind = the capacity for aspiration, devotion, reaching upward. (3) Sāma (left wing): the Sāma Veda — melodic chanting. The other wing = the capacity for harmony, beauty, aesthetic experience. Together the two wings = the mind's ability to soar through praise and melody. (4) Ādeśa (trunk): instruction/precept — the Brāhmaṇa prose that interprets and applies the mantras. The trunk/core of the mind = its capacity for UNDERSTANDING — not just receiving data but processing it into wisdom. (5) Atharva-Aṅgiras (tail/support): the Atharva Veda — practical, domestic, healing hymns. The support/foundation = the mind's engagement with everyday reality — health, household, protection, practical life. The teaching: the ideal mind is not a blank slate but a mind STRUCTURED by sacred knowledge — its governing principle (head) is purposeful action, its wings are praise and melody, its core is understanding, and its foundation is practical wisdom. The four Vedas aren't external texts — they are the architecture of the properly formed mind.

dp.q: 🔍 The progressive deepening — from food to mind
dp.a: The movement from annamaya to prāṇamaya to manomaya illustrates the Taittirīya's method of progressive interiorisation: The logic of each transition: (1) Annamaya → Prāṇamaya: the food-body is inert without breath. A corpse is made of food but has no life. Therefore breath (prāṇa) is more essential than food — it is the 'inner self' of the food-body. (2) Prāṇamaya → Manomaya: breath operates in deep sleep and even in coma — but without consciousness, without awareness. A person breathing but unconscious (in deep anaesthesia or coma) has prāṇa but no active mind. When mind returns, the person 'comes back.' Therefore mind (manas) is more essential than breath — it is the 'inner self' of the breath-body. The pattern: at each stage, the text asks: 'Is THIS the real self?' And answers: 'No — there is something more inner, more essential.' The food-body depends on breath; breath depends on mind; and as we'll see, mind depends on knowledge (vijñāna), and knowledge depends on bliss (ānanda). The Socratic parallel: this method resembles Socratic elenchus — each candidate for 'the real self' is examined, found wanting, and transcended. But unlike Socrates, the Taittirīya doesn't merely refute — it affirms each layer as real at its level while pointing to something deeper. The food-body IS you — but not ALL of you. Breath IS you — but not the deepest you. Mind IS you — but there's more.

sk: यतो वाचो निवर्तन्ते अप्राप्य मनसा सह आनन्दं ब्रह्मणो विद्वान् न बिभेति कुतश्चनेति तस्माद्वा एतस्मान्मनोमयात् अन्योऽन्तर आत्मा विज्ञानमयः तेनैष पूर्णः स वा एष पुरुषविध एव तस्य पुरुषविधताम् अन्वयं पुरुषविधः श्रद्धैव शिरः ऋतं दक्षिणः पक्षः सत्यमुत्तरः पक्षः योग आत्मा महः पुच्छं प्रतिष्ठा तदप्येष श्लोको भवति ||
ro: yataḥ · vācaḥ · nivartante · aprāpya · manasā · saha · ānandaṁ · brahmaṇaḥ · vidvān · na · bibheti · kutaścana · iti · tasmāt · vā · etasmāt · mano-mayāt · anyaḥ · antaraḥ · ātmā · vijñāna-mayaḥ · tena · eṣaḥ · pūrṇaḥ · saḥ · vā · eṣaḥ · puruṣa-vidhaḥ · eva · tasya · puruṣa-vidhatām · anvayaṁ · puruṣa-vidhaḥ · śraddhā · eva · śiraḥ · ṛtaṁ · dakṣiṇaḥ · pakṣaḥ · satyam · uttaraḥ · pakṣaḥ · yogaḥ · ātmā · mahaḥ · pucchaṁ · pratiṣṭhā · tat · api · eṣaḥ · ślokaḥ · bhavati ||
hi: जहाँ से (यतः) वाणी (speech / वाक्) निवर्तन्ते (turn back / लौट आती है) — मन (mind) सहित (सह) — [वहाँ तक] न पहुँच कर (अप्राप्य) — [जो] ब्रह्म (Brahman) का आनन्द (bliss) [जानता है] — विद्वान् (the knower / जानने वाला) न बिभेति (does not fear / भय नहीं करता) कुतश्चन (from anything whatsoever / किसी से भी)। उस (तस्मात्) इस (एतस्मात्) मनोमय (mind-self) से अन्य (another) अन्तर (inner) आत्मा (self) = विज्ञानमय (made of knowledge / विज्ञान से बना) है। उससे यह पूर्ण (filled) है। वह पुरुषविध (person-shaped) ही है। उसकी पुरुषविधता के अनुसार [यह भी] पुरुषविध है। श्रद्धा (faith / आस्था) ही (एव) [इसका] शिर (head)। ऋतम् (cosmic truth / ऋत) = दक्षिण पक्ष (right wing)। सत्यम् (truth / सत्य) = उत्तर पक्ष (left wing)। योग (yoga / concentration / एकाग्रता) = आत्मा (trunk / body)। महः (the Great / महान्) = पुच्छ प्रतिष्ठा (tail-support)। इस विषय में यह श्लोक है —
en: From where (yataḥ) speech (vāk) turns back (nivartante), together with (saha) the mind (manasā), unable to reach (aprāpya) [it] — the knower (vidvān) of the bliss (ānanda) of Brahman does not fear (na bibheti) from anything whatsoever (kutaścana). Other than this [self] made of mind, there is an inner self made of knowledge (vijñānamaya). By that, this [mind-self] is filled. That too is person-shaped. Conforming to its person-shape, this [inner self] is also person-shaped. Faith (śraddhā) is its head. Cosmic truth (ṛta) is the right wing. Truth (satya) is the left wing. Yoga (concentration) is the trunk (ātmā). Mahas (the Great) is the tail-support. Regarding this, there is this verse —

ws.h: जहाँ से वाणी लौट आती है / from where speech turns back
ws.e: from where speech turns back — yataḥ (from where) + vācaḥ (speech, plural) + nivartante (turn back/return); the famous declaration that Brahman is beyond the reach of speech — words cannot describe it, they 'turn back' unable to reach it; one of the most quoted Upanishadic phrases

ws.h: विज्ञान से बना / made of knowledge / made of discernment
ws.e: made of knowledge / discernment — vijñāna (vi + jñāna = special/discriminative knowledge) + maya (made of); the fourth kośa — deeper than mind (manas); vijñāna = the faculty of discernment, will, and direct knowing — what determines, decides, and understands; intellect in its higher function

ws.h: श्रद्धा / आस्था / faith / trust / conviction
ws.e: faith / trust / conviction — śrat (heart/truth) + √dhā (to place); literally 'placing one's heart in truth'; not blind belief but informed conviction — the willingness to commit to a path of inquiry; the HEAD of the vijñānamaya because without śraddhā, no deeper knowledge is possible

ws.h: योग / एकाग्रता / concentration / integration
ws.e: yoga / concentration / integration — from √yuj (to yoke/join); here = the concentrated, integrated state of consciousness; the TRUNK of the vijñānamaya because yoga (focused awareness) is the CORE of discerning knowledge — vijñāna requires concentrated attention

ws.h: किसी से भी भय नहीं करता / does not fear from anything whatsoever
ws.e: does not fear from anything whatsoever — the supreme fearlessness (abhaya) of the Brahman-knower; fear arises from duality — from seeing 'another' (the Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.2: 'dvitīyād vai bhayaṁ bhavati' — fear comes from a second); the knower of Brahman sees no second, therefore fears nothing

gr: The famous verse on Brahman's unreachability and the fourth sheath (vijñānamaya): this mantra contains one of the most quoted verses in all the Upanishads and introduces the fourth kośa. The verse — 'yato vāco nivartante': 'From where speech turns back, together with the mind, unable to reach — the knower of the bliss of Brahman does not fear from anything whatsoever.' This verse says two things: (a) Brahman is BEYOND speech and mind — words cannot describe it, thought cannot grasp it. (b) Yet the KNOWER of Brahman's bliss is completely fearless — knowing the infinite removes all fear. The paradox: Brahman cannot be reached by speech or mind — yet it CAN be known. How? Not through description or conceptualisation but through DIRECT EXPERIENCE — through being it, not thinking about it. The vijñānamaya kośa (knowledge-sheath): inside the manomaya is the vijñānamaya — the self made of vijñāna (discriminative knowledge / higher intellect). Its bird-parts are spiritual qualities, not Vedic texts: śraddhā (faith) = head, ṛta (cosmic truth) = right wing, satya (truth) = left wing, yoga (concentration) = trunk, mahas (the Great) = tail/support. The shift: the manomaya's bird-parts were the four Vedas (external scriptures). The vijñānamaya's bird-parts are INNER qualities — faith, truth, truth, concentration, greatness. This reflects the transition from external knowledge to internal realisation.
mt: REVIEW_NEEDED: taittiriya_upanishad_2.4.1-2.5.1 — The verse 'yato vāco nivartante aprāpya manasā saha' appears twice in the Taittirīya (here and again at 2.9.1), creating a frame around the bliss-analysis. It is one of the most frequently cited Upanishadic statements about Brahman's transcendence — echoed in the Kaṭha (1.3.15): 'aśabdam asparśam' (soundless, touchless), and the Kena (1.3): 'na tatra cakṣur gacchati' (the eye does not go there). The vijñānamaya kośa is philosophically crucial — it bridges the gap between ordinary mental activity (manomaya) and the bliss-self (ānandamaya). Vijñāna is distinguished from manas: manas = the processing mind that receives sense-data and forms thoughts; vijñāna = the discerning intellect that JUDGES, DECIDES, and KNOWS directly. In Shankara's reading, vijñāna = the agent of action and knowledge (kartṛ-bhokṛ). The bird-parts of the vijñānamaya — śraddhā, ṛta, satya, yoga, mahas — represent the qualities needed for liberation: faith to begin, cosmic and personal truth to guide, concentrated awareness to sustain, and greatness as the ground.

advaita.h: शंकर कहते हैं — 'यतो वाचो निवर्तन्ते' = ब्रह्म = वाक्-मनस्-अगोचर (beyond speech and mind)। विज्ञानमय = बुद्धि (intellect) = मन से सूक्ष्मतर — निश्चय (determination) + कर्तृत्व (agency)। श्रद्धा = शिर — क्योंकि बिना श्रद्धा के विज्ञान (knowledge) असम्भव। योग = आत्मा — एकाग्रता (concentration) = ज्ञान का सार (essence of knowledge)। परन्तु विज्ञानमय भी आत्मा (Self) नहीं — उसके भीतर आनन्दमय।
advaita.en: Shankara says 'yato vāco nivartante' = Brahman = beyond speech and mind. Vijñānamaya = intellect (buddhi) = subtler than mind — determination + agency. Śraddhā = head — because without faith, knowledge is impossible. Yoga = trunk — concentration = the essence of knowledge. But vijñānamaya is NOT the Self either — within it is the ānandamaya.
advaita.ins: Speech turns back. The mind turns back. Brahman is beyond both. Yet the one who KNOWS Brahman's bliss fears nothing — not because they've described it but because they've become it. Inside the mind-body is the knowledge-body — led by faith, winged by truth, centred on yoga. But even this is a sheath — there's one more layer.

vishisht.h: रामानुज कहते हैं — 'यतो वाचो निवर्तन्ते' = भगवान् = वाणी और मन से परे (beyond speech and mind) — परन्तु भक्ति (devotion) से प्राप्य (attainable through devotion)। विज्ञानमय = भगवान् का ज्ञान-रूप (God as knowledge)। श्रद्धा = शिर — भक्ति का प्रथम सोपान (first step of devotion)।
vishisht.en: Ramanuja says 'yato vāco nivartante' = God = beyond speech and mind — yet attainable through devotion (bhakti). Vijñānamaya = God as knowledge. Śraddhā = head — the first step of devotion.
vishisht.ins: God is beyond what words can say and what the mind can think. But the one who KNOWS His bliss fears nothing. Inside the mind is the knowledge-self — led by faith, the gateway to God. Faith is the head because without it, no deeper knowing begins.

aurobindo.h: श्री अरविन्द कहते हैं — 'यतो वाचो निवर्तन्ते' = ब्रह्म = मानसिक चेतना (mental consciousness) से परे — अतिमानसिक (supramental) क्षेत्र में। विज्ञानमय = विज्ञान-चेतना (truth-consciousness / सत्य-चेतना) — मन से ऊपर का स्तर। श्रद्धा = अन्तर्ज्ञान में विश्वास (trust in inner knowledge)। योग = चेतना का एकीकरण (integration of consciousness)।
aurobindo.en: Sri Aurobindo says 'yato vāco nivartante' = Brahman = beyond mental consciousness — in the supramental domain. Vijñānamaya = truth-consciousness — the plane above mind. Śraddhā = trust in inner knowledge. Yoga = integration of consciousness.
aurobindo.ins: Speech and mind turn back — Brahman is beyond the mental plane. The knowledge-sheath is the faculty that reaches beyond mind toward truth-consciousness. Its head is faith — not blind belief but the inner conviction that truth exists beyond thought. Its core is yoga — the integration that makes direct knowing possible.

dp.q: 🔍 'Yato vāco nivartante' — beyond speech and mind
dp.a: The verse 'yato vāco nivartante aprāpya manasā saha' ('from where speech turns back, together with the mind, unable to reach') is one of the most important statements about Brahman's nature in the Upanishadic corpus: The claim: Brahman cannot be reached by speech (vāk) or mind (manas). Both TURN BACK — they try to reach Brahman and fail, returning empty-handed. Speech cannot describe Brahman because Brahman is not an object with qualities that words can capture. Mind cannot think Brahman because Brahman is not a concept the intellect can frame. The parallels: (a) Kena 1.3: 'na tatra cakṣur gacchati, na vāg gacchati, no manaḥ' (the eye does not go there, nor speech, nor the mind). (b) Kaṭha 1.3.15: 'aśabdam asparśam arūpam avyayam' (soundless, touchless, formless, imperishable). (c) Bṛhadāraṇyaka 2.3.6: 'neti neti' (not this, not this) — Brahman is defined by negation. The paradox resolved: if Brahman is beyond speech and mind, how can it be KNOWN? The verse itself answers: 'ānandaṁ brahmaṇo vidvān' — the KNOWER of Brahman's bliss does not fear. Brahman IS known — but not through description or conceptualisation. It is known through BEING — through direct identity. The vijñānamaya kośa represents this transition: from mind (which processes concepts) to vijñāna (which directly discerns reality). The fearlessness: 'na bibheti kutaścana' — the knower fears NOTHING. Why? Because fear requires a 'second' (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 1.4.2: 'dvitīyād vai bhayaṁ bhavati'). The knower of Brahman sees no second — everything is Brahman. No enemy, no death, no loss — because there is nothing OTHER than what they are.

dp.q: 🔍 The vijñānamaya kośa — from information to realisation
dp.a: The vijñānamaya kośa (knowledge-sheath) marks a critical transition in the five-sheath analysis — from processing (manomaya) to knowing (vijñānamaya): Manas vs. vijñāna: (a) Manas (mind): receives sense-data, forms thoughts, has doubts, considers options. It is the PROCESSING faculty — it thinks ABOUT things. (b) Vijñāna (knowledge/discernment): determines, decides, knows directly. It is the KNOWING faculty — it doesn't think about reality, it GRASPS reality. In Advaita terms, vijñāna = buddhi (intellect) in its higher function. In Aurobindo's terms, vijñāna = truth-consciousness, the faculty that directly perceives truth. The bird-parts reveal the shift: the manomaya's parts were external (four Vedas — scripture). The vijñānamaya's parts are INTERNAL QUALITIES: (1) Śraddhā (faith) = head: the governing principle of knowledge is FAITH — not blind belief but the deep conviction that truth exists and can be known. Without śraddhā, the seeker gives up before reaching vijñāna. (2) Ṛta (cosmic truth) = right wing: alignment with the objective order of reality. (3) Satya (truth) = left wing: alignment with truthful expression and honest inquiry. (4) Yoga (concentration) = trunk: the CORE of vijñāna is yoga — focused, integrated awareness. Vijñāna is not scattered thinking but concentrated knowing. (5) Mahas (the Great) = support: the vijñānamaya rests on 'greatness' — the expansive ground of being. Why this matters: the vijñānamaya represents the point where the seeker transitions from LEARNING ABOUT Brahman (through study, concepts, scriptures) to KNOWING Brahman (through direct discernment). It is the last 'sheath' before the ānandamaya — the bliss-body that borders on Brahman itself.
